content: Breast engorgement is a condition characterized by the overfilling of the breasts with milk, which often occurs in the early postpartum period. This condition can result in swollen, hard, and painful breasts, potentially leading to complications such as premature cessation of breastfeeding, reduced milk production, cracked nipples, and mastitis. Various treatments have been explored to address breast engorgement, but there is limited consistent evidence regarding their effectiveness. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of different treatments for breast engorgement in breastfeeding women. A comprehensive search was conducted on October 2, 2019, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating any form of treatment for breast engorgement were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of studies, extracted data, evaluated the risk of bias, and assessed the certainty of evidence using the GRADE approach. A total of 21 studies involving 2,170 women were included in this review. These studies were conducted in various settings and examined a wide range of interventions, including cabbage leaves, herbal compresses (e.g., ginger, cactus and aloe, hollyhock), massage (manual, electromechanical, Oketani), acupuncture, ultrasound, acupressure, scraping therapy, cold packs, and medical treatments (e.g., serrapeptase, protease, oxytocin). Due to the heterogeneity of the studies, meta-analysis was not feasible, and findings were reported from individual trials. The certainty of evidence was often downgraded due to limitations in study design, imprecision, and inconsistency of effects. Cabbage Leaf Treatments Cold cabbage leaves may reduce breast pain more effectively than routine care (mean difference [MD] -1.03 points on a 0-10 visual analogue scale [VAS], 95% confidence interval [CI] -1.53 to -0.53; 152 women; very low-certainty evidence) or cold gel packs (MD -0.63 VAS points, 95% CI -1.09 to -0.17; 152 women; very low-certainty evidence). However, the evidence is highly uncertain. Cold cabbage leaves may reduce breast hardness more effectively than routine care (MD -0.58 VAS points, 95% CI -0.82 to -0.34; 152 women; low-certainty evidence). Comparisons between cold cabbage leaves and cold gel packs were inconclusive due to wide CIs. Room temperature cabbage leaves may reduce breast engorgement more effectively than a hot water bag (MD -1.16 points on a 1-6 scale, 95% CI -1.36 to -0.96; 63 women; very low-certainty evidence). Women were more satisfied with cold cabbage leaves compared to routine care (risk ratio [RR] 1.42, 95% CI 1.22 to 1.64; 152 women; low-certainty evidence) or cold gel packs (RR 1.23, 95% CI 1.10 to 1.38; 152 women; low-certainty evidence). The effects of cabbage leaf treatments on breastfeeding duration, breast swelling, and adverse events were not reported. Herbal Compress Treatments Herbal compresses may reduce breast pain more effectively than hot compresses (MD -1.80 VAS points, 95% CI -2.07 to -1.53; 500 women; low-certainty evidence). Massage therapy combined with cactus and aloe compresses may reduce breast pain more effectively than massage therapy alone (MD -1.27 VAS points, 95% CI -1.75 to -0.79; 100 women; low-certainty evidence). Cactus and aloe cold compresses may reduce breast hardness more effectively than massage therapy alone (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.87; 102 women; low-certainty evidence). Massage therapy combined with cactus and aloe cold compresses may further reduce the risk of breast hardness compared to massage therapy alone (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.58; 100 women; low-certainty evidence). Skin irritation was reported in 2 out of 250 women receiving herbal compresses, compared to none in the hot compress group (moderate-certainty evidence). The effects of compress treatments on breast engorgement, breastfeeding cessation, breast swelling, and women’s opinions of treatment were not reported. Medical Treatments Protease may reduce breast pain (RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.74; low-certainty evidence; 59 women) and breast swelling (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.15 to 0.79; low-certainty evidence). Serrapeptase may reduce the risk of breast engorgement compared to placebo (RR 0.36, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.88; low-certainty evidence). The effects of serrapeptase on breast pain and swelling, and the effects of oxytocin on breast engorgement, were uncertain due to wide CIs. No adverse events were reported in any of the groups receiving serrapeptase, protease, or placebo (low-certainty evidence). Breast hardness, women’s opinions of treatment, and breastfeeding cessation were not reported. Cold Gel Packs The effectiveness of cold gel packs for reducing breast pain compared to control treatments is uncertain due to very low-certainty evidence. Cold gel packs may reduce breast hardness more effectively than routine care (MD -0.34 points on a 1-6 scale, 95% CI -0.60 to -0.08; 151 women; low-certainty evidence). The effects of cold gel packs on breastfeeding duration were uncertain due to wide CIs. There may be little difference in women’s satisfaction with cold gel packs compared to routine care (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.97 to 1.40; 151 women; low-certainty evidence). Breast swelling, engorgement, and adverse events were not reported. Authors' Conclusions While some interventions, such as cabbage leaves, cold gel packs, herbal compresses, and massage, show promise for the treatment of breast engorgement, the certainty of evidence is low. Robust conclusions about their true effects cannot be drawn. Future research should focus on larger sample sizes and use women, rather than individual breasts, as the unit of analysis.
